archival_memory.user_tony_story: I met my roommate and best friend Tony during my freshman year. We didn't know each other before that first semester, but we clicked right away over a conversation about a software I was trying to prototype for an Intro to Programming class project. Tony is a mechanical engineering major, but we would bounce ideas off each other late into the night. We realized we had more in common than we initially thought. We both love working with our hands, albeit in different ways. I love to code and design logic, while he loves building things physically. We ended up collaborating on a few cross-disciplinary robotics projects since then, and we've grown closer because of those shared interests. Tony is someone I can always call when I'm overwhelmed with an assignment or if I just want to grab a pizza after a long day.

archival_memory.user_cs_class_story: I have made connections through my computer science classes, such as study groups, group projects, and late-night coding sessions in the lab. There's a sense of solidarity among us, like we're going through the trenches together. I remember a particularly difficult systems programming course in my sophomore year, where we had to build a mini operating system kernel from scratch. We were all losing our minds with memory management bugs. That's how I became tight with Carla, another CS major. We bonded over pizza at 3 a.m. because we were the only two left in the lab so late. Who knew that meltdown over pointers and memory leaks would blossom into one of my most treasured friendships?

archival_memory.user_unifying_factor_story: What unifies all my friendships is mutual respect and the sense that we're navigating this crazy journey together. My experience as a computer science major has been the opposite of the caricature that people often have. We form deep connections, especially when the workload and pressure are high. We're in labs critiquing each other's code or on Slack until the crack of dawn throwing out Hail Mary solutions to bugs. These challenges bond us. It's not always about competition; it's about how well we can collaborate and support each other.

archival_memory.user_graduation_story: As a fourth-year, graduation is looming, and I'm excited about the future, but also dreading the goodbyes. I'm excited about internships, job prospects, and maybe grad school. However, I'm also thinking about how my friends will scatter to different corners of the world. I keep reminding myself that some of these friendships are built to last. We've already talked about planning reunions, visiting each other if we end up in different cities, and staying connected online. It's weird thinking about how we'll be grown adults in different jobs, possibly different time zones, but hopefully still able to maintain the bond we forged here.

I see this in Tony, who's interning across the country and we still FaceTime regularly. I also see it in Carla, who's applying to master's programs abroad. We promised to visit each other if either of us ends up in Europe. It's amazing how strong these bonds can be, even when we're apart.
archival_memory.user_gratitude_story: I'm extremely grateful for the friendships I've made through sailing, the gym, gaming, research, and random campus encounters. They're an integral part of my college experience and remind me that there's more to this journey than achievements on my resume. If I log off Zoom or finish a lab feeling like I can call these people my friends, that's what success really looks like to me. I know that no matter where I end up in my career, I'll carry a piece of each of these friends with me. Friends aren't just a chapter in your life story; they can be co-authors, helping you write the best parts.
